clinical_category: Inflammatory arthritis evaluation - ESR and CRP interpretation
blueprint_topic: Interpretation of nonspecific inflammatory laboratory markers
stem: A client with joint pain and swelling has elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP). Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: The elevated markers support the presence of inflammation but do not identify a specific diagnosis by themselves; they must be interpreted with the clinical examination and other testing.
options.B: The elevated ESR and CRP confirm rheumatoid arthritis regardless of the joint pattern, autoantibody results, or other possible causes of inflammation.
options.C: ESR and CRP are unrelated to inflammatory disease and therefore should be ignored when evaluating joint symptoms.
options.D: Once ESR and CRP are elevated, no additional laboratory, imaging, or clinical assessment is needed because the cause has been established.

rationale: A is correct. Current NIAMS guidance describes ESR and CRP as laboratory measures of inflammation that can help evaluate rheumatoid arthritis and monitor disease activity, but rheumatoid arthritis has no single diagnostic test and diagnosis relies on the history, physical examination, laboratory findings, and imaging as appropriate. Elevated inflammatory markers therefore support an inflammatory process but are not disease-specific. B incorrectly treats nonspecific markers as diagnostic for RA. C denies their established clinical role. D incorrectly substitutes inflammatory-marker elevation for a complete diagnostic evaluation. The final item focuses on appropriate laboratory interpretation and avoids unsupported numerical cutoffs.
educational_objective: Interpret elevated ESR and CRP as evidence supporting systemic inflammation while recognizing that these markers are nonspecific and require correlation with clinical findings and other diagnostic data.
source_organization: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Rheumatoid Arthritis: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Steps to Take
source_locator: NIAMS 'Rheumatoid Arthritis: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Steps to Take' → Diagnosis: RA has no single diagnostic test and clinicians use history, physical examination, laboratory tests and imaging. Laboratory Tests → ESR measures inflammation and CRP is another common test for inflammation; both can help diagnose RA and monitor disease activity/response but are interpreted with the broader evaluation.
source_claim_supported: Current NIAMS guidance directly supports ESR and CRP as inflammatory markers used within a broader rheumatoid-arthritis evaluation rather than as stand-alone disease-specific diagnostic tests.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Reduction of Risk Potential: monitor and interpret diagnostic and laboratory findings, compare client data with expected findings, and recognize when further evaluation is required.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's abstract marker-description item into a laboratory-interpretation question. The final version uses current NIH/NIAMS guidance, preserves the established role of ESR/CRP in inflammation assessment, and prevents disease-specific diagnostic certainty or replacement of the broader evaluation.
audit_findings: The source's core concept was valid but low-discrimination and used a generic rheumatology citation.
Fresh NIAMS review directly supports ESR/CRP as inflammation measures used alongside the rest of the RA diagnostic evaluation.
The final item explicitly prevents elevated inflammatory markers from being treated as a disease-specific diagnosis.
Distractors test RA certainty, dismissal of inflammatory markers, and replacement of the broader diagnostic workup; none is defensible.
